Tokyo summoned Russia’s ambassador after a Japanese reporter was arrested in Russia’s far east and accused of collecting military intelligence.

Listen

![Image 1: A building with a facade of light-colored panels and dark glass. Power lines and trees are visible in the foreground along the street.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14int-japan-journalist-pqfl/14int-japan-journalist-pqfl-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper headquarters in Sapporo, Japan on Wednesday. A journalist from the newspaper was arrested in Russia and accused of spying.Credit...Kyodo, via Reuters

Oct. 14, 2026, 7:29 a.m. ET

The Japanese government on Wednesday protested [Russia’s detention of a Japanese journalist](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/russia-detains-japanese-journalist.html) accused of spying, calling on Moscow to provide “humane, fair, and impartial” treatment to the reporter.

The protest came after Russia’s main security agency said on Tuesday that the authorities had detained a Japanese journalist, accusing him of collecting intelligence on Russia’s military capabilities. The journalist, whose name has not been released, worked as a foreign correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun, a newspaper based on Japan’s northernmost island.

Japan’s Foreign Ministry said it had summoned Russia’s ambassador to Japan, Nikolay Stanislavovich Nozdrev, to lodge a “strong protest.” The ministry said in a statement that Japan had received “no explanation whatsoever regarding the detained national.”

Russia’s Federal Security Service, or F.S.B., said in a statement on Tuesday that the journalist was arrested in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the Pacific island of Sakhalin in eastern Russia. It said the journalist had been transported to Moscow, where he was remanded into pretrial custody by the Lefortovo District Court.

The F.S.B. accused the journalist of collecting data on the number of local recruits taking part in the war in Ukraine, according to the Russian news agency Tass.

The incident was the latest flare-up in tensions between Russia and Japan. In August, President Vladimir V. Putin made his [first ever](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/13/world/asia/putin-visit-islands-japan-russia.html) visit to islands claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo, prompting an angry rebuke from Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

Russia has been engaged in a long-running dispute with Japan over the islands, which are part of an archipelago stretching from the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula in eastern Russia to Hokkaido in northern Japan.

Moscow administers the disputed islands from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, where the journalist was arrested.

The fight over the archipelago, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and in Russia as the southern Kuril Islands, has festered since 1945, when Moscow seized the territory from Japan in the final weeks of World War II.

Ms. Takaichi called Mr. Putin’s visit in August “absolutely unacceptable” and said he “hurt the feelings of the Japanese people.”

In September, Mr. Putin said that “everything that is happening now, the deterioration in our relationship, is entirely down to the Japanese government.”

Russia has accused Japan of seeking to revive World War II era militarism by embarking on an effort to strengthen its defense forces. Japanese officials say the changes are necessary to counter rising threats from China, Russia and North Korea.

Mr. Putin has been angered by Japan’s decision to join Western allies in punishing Russia over its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ms. Takaichi’s government this month imposed new sanctions, taking aim at shadow vessels linked to Moscow’s illicit oil trade.

The Hokkaido Shimbun did not disclose details about the journalist on Wednesday but said in a statement that it was aware of the detention.

“We are currently verifying the details,” the newspaper said. “Our top priority is ensuring the reporter’s safety.”

James D.J. Brown, a professor of political science at Temple University in Tokyo, said the charges against the journalist appeared to be political, noting that Japan does not even have a dedicated foreign intelligence service.

“Rather than thinking of it as a real espionage case,” he said, “it’s better to think of it as a political case and essentially hostage diplomacy.”

Still, Professor Brown said it was unclear if Japan would take forceful action against Russia over the detention. Japanese leaders have historically sought stable relations with Moscow; Japan depends on Russia for about 10 percent of its liquefied natural gas imports.

“I fear instead that they’re going to try and deal with it behind the scenes,” he said. “They will continue their sort of softly softly approach. There will be voices in Japan saying, ‘Don’t poke the bear, don’t provoke Russia, and everything will be fine.’”

In March 2023, a Wall Street Journal reporter, [Evan Gershkovich](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/evan-gershkovich-interview.html), was arrested in the city of Yekaterinburg and accused of spying for the United States, which he and The Journal denied. He was sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in August 2024 as part of the largest prisoner swap since the fall of the Soviet Union.

Hisako Ueno contributed reporting.

[Javier C. Hernández](https://www.nytimes.com/by/javier-c-hernandez) is the Tokyo bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Japan and the region. He has reported from Asia for much of the past decade, previously serving as China correspondent in Beijing.

Title: Argentina’s President Has a Dog Psychic. Meet Celia Melamed.

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/americas/argentina-president-milei-dog-pet-psychic.html

Published Time: 2026-10-14T09:00:10.000Z

The Global Profile

In Argentina, many people try to read the mind of the president. Celia Melamed read the mind of his dogs.

Listen

· 9:15 min

![Image 1: A person sits in a chair with her back to a desk with piles of paper. Curtains cover a window.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/07/world/00int-argentina-psychic-profile/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Celia Melamed, a pet psychic, was hired by President Javier Milei of Argentina to talk to his dogs. Credit...Sarah Pabst for The New York Times

Oct. 14, 2026, 5:00 a.m. ET

At first, there was nothing unusual about Celia Melamed’s new client. His English mastiff was dying, so he hired her to read its mind.

But when she met the man with the messy hair, he kept apologizing for his casual outfit. “He told me, ‘Sorry for being dressed like this; I’m always in a suit on television,’” recalled Ms. Melamed. “I don’t have a television, so I had no idea what he was talking about.”

The man was Javier Milei, at the time a TV pundit in Argentina known for railing against the government. The mastiff was Conan, soon to be Argentina’s most famous dog. And Ms. Melamed, by extension, was about to become the nation’s most well-known animal psychic.

That is because, a few years later, Mr. Milei was elected Argentina’s president, and Conan was a symbol of his brash campaign, as well as the genetic model for the handful of clones that are now the nation’s first dogs.

But in that first encounter about a decade ago, Conan was on his deathbed, and Ms. Melamed said she was communicating with him via an energy she felt in her chest. She said she relayed Mr. Milei’s message that he was desperately trying to save the dog.

“What I remember is that he felt better afterward,” she said of Mr. Milei. “Few people have such an intense connection with their animals.”

Ms. Melamed then became his dedicated pet psychic. He kept hiring her for the next two years, she said, including to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. They stopped working together a few years before Mr. Milei was elected president in 2023.

Mr. Milei and his spokesmen did not respond to requests for comment. He has long made clear that he views his dogs as more than just pets. Mr. Milei, who is unmarried and childless, refers to them as his children, and his press secretary has admonished reporters who ask about the animals, saying it is equivalent to snooping into his family.

Image

![Image 2: A silver gavel engraved with "CONAN MILTON MURRAY" rests on a brown wooden surface. Next to it, a folded blue and white striped fabric lies, with a blurry person visible behind.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/09/multimedia/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-tgjq/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-tgjq-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A photo released by the Argentine Senate shows a detailed view of the presidential baton, which depicts Mr. Milei’s five dogs.Credit...Luciano Ingaramo/Argentine Senate

As a result, the dogs have become a central mystery of Mr. Milei’s presidency. Only one has been seen publicly since he was elected president, and there have been frequent rumors that others have died. When Mr. Milei suddenly [fired](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-18/milei-fires-presidential-residence-staff-over-security-nacion-says) much of the presidential residence’s staff last month, Argentine pundits [speculated](https://youtu.be/Cr74bV8MkGY?si=Cc-LTwlJtb9mV3UY&t=224) the move had something to do with his dogs, which he has said are kept in separate kennels there.

It has even become common political fodder in Argentina that Mr. Milei seeks out his dogs for advice. A top foreign diplomat and a longtime friend of Mr. Milei’s, both of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said they have heard Mr. Milei say so.

When asked by journalists about the claim, Mr. Milei has responded coyly, saying what happens in his house is private. “If he gives me advice, he’s a genius,” Mr. Milei said in 2023, referring to Conan. (Although Conan died in 2017, Mr. Milei has suggested that one of the clones is Conan’s reincarnation.)

Image

![Image 3: A person wearing a gray and blue top sits next to a tan dog with its tongue out.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/08/multimedia/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-qwpl/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-qwpl-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A rare public appearance of one of Mr. Milei’s dogs during an interview he gave in 2025.Credit...Office of the Argentine President

Asked whether she delivered a dog’s counsel to the future president, Ms. Melamed cited client privacy.

Mr. Milei is hardly her only client. After her work for him [became public](https://www.clarin.com/cultura/perros-milei-dios-juan-luis-gonzalez-desnuda-fuerzas-cielo-conexion-mistica-presidente_0_dZSL0IbfGm.html) a few years ago, her wait-list ballooned to two months, she said.

From her tiny Buenos Aires apartment draped in wind chimes and dream catchers, Ms. Melamed, 67, charges pet owners $35 an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds to find out what is ailing the animals, where they are hiding or how they are doing in the afterlife. She says she needs merely a photo of an animal to perceive its emotions and thoughts, typically via sensations in her body.

“How does it work?” she said. “I don’t know. I only know that it works.”

She represents what appears to be increasing global interest in the business of pet telepathy, notwithstanding an absence of scientific evidence.

While there are no reliable statistics on the industry, self-proclaimed animal communicators and their clients have proliferated on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram. Popular animal communicators on social media say business is booming.

“When I started out, I was pretty much alone,” said Cindy Brody, a communicator from Woodstock, N.Y., who has been in the business for nearly 40 years. Interest took off several years ago, she said, and now her wait-list is nearly a month long. She holds up to 20 sessions per week, charging $275 an hour. “It’s our time now,” she said.

Clara Martín, an animal communicator from Madrid, said her clients are also multiplying, including a wild-animal sanctuary in South Africa and a man living with 23 cats in Japan. “People understand their animals have something to say,” she said.

Ms. Melamed said she first noticed her powerful intuition as a child when she could predict correct answers in guessing games. But she never cultivated those abilities during a career in veterinary medicine and bacteriology. Then, in 2008, she read a book about communicating with animals and began taking courses.

Image

![Image 4: A person sits on a patterned bed, hands clasped to their chest, mouth slightly open. Sunlight streams from a window.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/07/multimedia/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-bvtk/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-bvtk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Ms. Melamed said she can communicate with an animal via sensations in her body, simply by looking at a photo of the animal.Credit...Sarah Pabst for The New York Times

Two years later, a horse she was working with stepped on her, but when she telepathically forgave it, she said her pain went away. “I realized there was something much deeper going on,” she said.

Over two visits to her home, I watched Ms. Melamed work. (Since the Covid-19 pandemic, she has read animals’ minds remotely.) She looked at photos of cats and dogs, closed her eyes and, according to her, connected with the animals almost instantaneously. Stressed animals can make her body feel tense, she said, while lost pets have made her smell things that provide a clue to their whereabouts.

“Sometimes what I feel is difficult to put into words,” she said. “I try to be as reliable as possible.”

In one case, she said she asked a dog with persistent diarrhea if it had a message for its owner. “‘Tell her that I’m not her grandmother,’” Ms. Melamed recalled the dog responding. The owner was stunned, she said, and admitted she had called the dog her grandmother’s name because of its gait, but would stop. “From that communication onward, the dog stopped having bloody diarrhea,” Ms. Melamed said.

Clara Quattrucci, 65, said she began booking regular appointments with Ms. Melamed two years ago after she helped her cocker spaniel, Mía, recover from the emotional trauma of an attack from another dog. “It honestly blew my mind,” she said.

Image

![Image 5: A person sits at a desk in front of a laptop where another person is on video. An image of a dog is on a cellphone next to the laptop.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/07/world/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-02/00int-argentina-psychic-profile-02-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Ms. Melamed on a call with her client, Clara Quattrucci. A photo of Ms. Quattrucci’s cocker spaniel, Mía, is on display so that Ms. Melamed can connect telepathically with the animal, she said.Credit...Sarah Pabst for The New York Times

Dozens of people now advertise pet-psychic services in Buenos Aires, up from just a handful a decade ago, she said. That is in part thanks to Ms. Melamed. She estimates she has trained about 700 people in her pet-communication workshops.

“We’re all capable,’’ she said. “The only thing that blocks us is our belief we can’

· 2:50 min

![Image 1: A person in a dark coat stands looking down, near a tall white marble statue of a robed figure holding a cross. A large building with many lit windows forms the background.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14int-pope-dispatch-gkmj/14int-pope-dispatch-gkmj-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A statue of Pope John Paul II outside the hospital in Rome where Pope Leo XIV was hospitalized. The statue has become a gathering point for prayers.Credit...Stoyan Nenov/Reuters

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 7:56 a.m. ET

Patients and well-wishers alike came to offer prayers Wednesday on the grounds of the Rome hospital where Pope Leo XIV was recovering from [surgery that found lung cancer](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/pope-leo-lung-surgery.html).

“Hematology greets the pope” read a poster hung from one window of the hospital, Policlinico A. Gemelli. Below, a banner saying “Long Live the Pope” was laid out on a bench in the sun.

Leo, 71, is expected to spend about a week in the hospital, a huge complex in northwestern Rome. Just outside the main entrance, votive candles, prayer cards, a plaster cherub and a miniature orchid decorated a statue of Pope John Paul II. Several people filtered through, some falling to their knees.

Fernando Ibarra Mendoza, 41, read a prayer for healing in front of the statue as her 6-year-old daughter drew a card for Pope Leo with pink highlighters.

“Pope Leo needs our prayer, and the church, and the world, needs Pope Leo,” Ms. Ibarra Mendoza said. “In these dark times, we pilgrims must be near to him.”

Mariana Nicula Ancuta, 48, also stopped by the statue after her appointment.

“Gemelli is a marvelous hospital, which took out tumors in both of my breasts,” she said. “I know that he’s in the right hands, in the best hands in the world.”

Surgeons [removed the lower lobe](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/pope-leo-lung-surgery.html) of the pope’s right lung on Tuesday after finding a cancerous nodule. The Vatican has not said whether the pope will undergo further treatment.

Simona Zanfrilli, 45, came to pray for Leo after her chemotherapy session and said that she hoped he would not require the same “devastating” treatment. Ms. Zanfrilli said she thought, though, that the pope’s diagnosis could offer fellow cancer patients comfort and even hope.

“It sounds strange,” she said, “but this morning during my treatment, I felt almost lucky. I thought: I’m in the same place, on the same floor, even, as the Holy Father.”

The cancer diagnosis came only about a year and a half into Leo’s papacy — the [first American pope](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/11/world/europe/conclave-vote-pope-leo-robert-prevost.html), he was elected to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025. That weighed heavy on the mind of Giuseppe Antonio Perazzo, 76, who came to the hospital before his lunch.

Gemelli was where Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, spent weeks receiving treatment shortly before [his death](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/21/world/europe/pope-francis-dead.html).

“It’s much too soon to re-elect a new Holy Father,” said Mr. Perazzo, “so I’m praying that he can recover.”

## France Loses More Precious Art With Theft of Dalí Book Cover

Three thieves broke into a private museum in central France and took off with a 330-pound book cover created by the surrealist master Salvador Dalí.

Listen

· 5:24 min

![Image 1: An ornate book cover made of bronze.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/15/multimedia/13int-france-dali-photo-cvjf/13int-france-dali-photo-cvjf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

The cover of the “Book of Revelation,” which was created by Salvador Dalí.Credit...Thierry Zoccolan/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 10:15 a.m. ET

Books should not be judged by their covers — unless the cover is a 330-pound, jewel-encrusted sculpture created by the master surrealist Salvador Dalí. In that case, it may also appeal to art thieves, as a recent heist in France revealed.

The “Book of Revelation,” or “Livre de l’Apocalypse,” was a literary art project involving 14 prominent modern artists and writers, including Jean Cocteau. First shown in 1961 at the Museum of Modern Art of Paris, it was considered the world’s most expensive book at the time.

Of late, the cover has been on permanent display at a private museum in Issoire, in central France. At least until last week, when three thieves broke in and took off with the unwieldy work, leaving behind broken glass and shadowy images captured by security cameras.

The theft of the Dalí comes amid a rash of art heists in France, including at the Louvre in Paris last year and at a museum in the country’s south dedicated to the painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir last month. That has raised alarm about the security of other valuable works.

“It is a monumental loss,” said Nathanaël Molay, who has spent 20 years working with the book’s owner, Christian Karoutzos, an artist, restorer, collector and owner of the C Karoutzos Contemporary Art Center, the private museum in Issoire.

The two men, who recently completed a 385-page text analyzing the artwork, were on the phone when Mr. Karoutzos discovered the theft, Mr. Molay said. The owner, he said, is “devastated” and asked him to respond to queries in his stead.

“It’s like losing someone you love,” he said.

The precise monetary value of the stolen book cover is unclear. Mr. Molay estimated that it is worth at least several million dollars, based on its technical and artistic uniqueness and the prices fetched by smaller, less distinctive works by Dalí.

“The work is exceptional,” Mr. Molay said.

The stolen cover is made of bronze and cast using a [“lost wax” technique](https://pages.ucsd.edu/~dkjordan/cgi-bin/moreabout.pl?tyimuh=lostwax) that makes it impossible to recreate.

The police have been to the museum, dusting it for fingerprints and analyzing both the site and security camera footage. Now they are looking for clues, including who may have visited the museum website before the heist, Mr. Molay said. He said that he had spoken with investigators on Tuesday, more than a week after the theft, but that there was still “little known” about the crime.

A French art publisher, Joseph Forêt, came up with the idea for the “Book of Revelation” collaboration in 1958 and recruited the artists and writers involved. After, its completion in 1961, it was [displayed at museums](https://www.nytimes.com/1964/04/16/archives/quarterton-volume-arrives-for-the-fair.html) around the world, but eventually faded from view.

Mr. Karoutzos acquired the work in 2003 and has been studying it ever since. Most of the book, made up of 150 parchment pages with art and writing, was not on display — the museum is too small for such an extensive exhibition, Mr. Molay said — and remains safe. But in the owner’s estimation, the cover was unlike any other art object in existence, and an important gateway to the greater project.

In the text analyzing the “Book of the Apocalypse,” which the museum plans to publish as a book, Mr. Karoutzos says it can be compared to a cathedral because it combines the skills of writers, artists, crafts people, calligraphers and other specialists.

“If one were to single out the most spectacular element of this monumental work,” he writes, “the cover designed by Salvador Dalí would naturally stand out.”

The cover stands in contrast to many other works by Dalí because it is one of a kind.

Dalí is considered one of the most widely reproduced and faked artists, a master who damaged his reputation and contributed to confusion in the market for his works by [signing blank sheets of paper](https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/26/world/dali-trying-to-repair-business-affairs-and-resolve-art-scandals.html) en masse. In 1974, the French customs police halted a truck loaded with 40,000 blank pieces of paper signed by Dalí; the year before, a French notary affirmed that Dalí had signed 4,000 sheets of paper at a hotel in Paris in preparation for future sales.

The cover of the “Book of Revelation” is impossible to reproduce because its original wax model melted away during the casting process. It would also be difficult for thieves to sell in its original form, which raises concerns that the bronze cover with precious stones, pearls, seashells, needles, knives, forks and more may be destroyed, Mr. Molay said.

This is not the first Dalí theft to generate headlines in recent decades.

In 2012, a [New York gallery visitor](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/23/nyregion/theft-of-a-drawing-by-dali-was-incongruous-in-its-simplicity.html) casually left an exhibition with a drawing by the artist valued at about $150,000. A Dalí painting donated to Rikers Island in 1965 because the artist was unable to attend a painting session with inmates as he had promised, was displayed at the jail until it was stolen by guards during a fire drill in 2003.

[Ephrat Livni](https://www.nytimes.com/by/ephrat-livni) is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

### [Here’s the latest.](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/14/business/inflation-cpi-report-september/heres-the-latest#heres-the-latest)

Higher energy prices drove up inflation in the United States in September, a warning shot to President Trump ahead of midterm elections that have centered primarily on affordability concerns. The uptick in consumer prices will also keep the Federal Reserve under pressure to raise interest rates again after last month’s move.

The Consumer Price Index Report, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday, showed overall prices rose 0.6 percent, the largest monthly increase in five months. Compared with the same time last year, prices were 3.7 percent higher.

The bulk of the increase stemmed directly from energy prices, which have shot higher this year because of the war with Iran. Gasoline prices, which in late September rose to the highest level in four months at nearly $4.50 a gallon, surged 9.1 percent for the month. That accounted for more than half of the overall monthly increase in prices. They are up 34.2 percent over the past year.

Fuel oil prices, used for heating in many homes in the northeast, have also shot higher, rising 15.3 percent in September, or 74.2 percent on an annual basis.

“Core” inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, edged higher as well, but by a smaller magnitude. Over the course of September, these prices were up only 0.3 percent. Over the past year, they were up 2.6 percent.

Here’s what else to know:

*   **Price pressures:** Inflation has surged over the past year not only because of the Iran war, but also President Trump’s tariffs and soaring costs associated with the boom in artificial intelligence investment. In September, the primary driver of price pressures was energy prices, which on the whole rose 5.2 percent for the month, or 20.4 percent over the past year. Higher fuel costs are driving up airfares, which were up 1.2 percent in September and 22.4 percent over the year.

*   **Tariffs still hitting certain sectors:** Prices on toys were up 4.2 percent in September. But other categories that are heavily exposed to tariffs showed fairly minimal effects. Apparel was up 0.3 percent last month, and prices on household furnishings fell 0.2 percent. Spending on the A.I. buildout helped to push up prices for computers and related equipment by 9.7 percent over the past year. Software prices have risen 28.4 percent over that time period. Still, smartphone prices have fallen nearly 10 percent.

*   **Zero wage growth:** The combination of higher inflation and weaker wage growth means that Americans are earning less for every hour of work. Average hourly earnings, adjusted for inflation, fell 0.5 percent in August, and were down 0.7 percent from a year earlier. It was the sixth straight months of year-over-year declines in real earnings. Average hourly earnings are now back to almost exactly where they were when President Trump was sworn into office for the second time, meaning that, on average, Americans have experienced zero wage growth, in real terms, since he returned to the White House.

*   **Fed watch:** Fed officials pay closest attention to the core measure, which they see as the best gauge of underlying inflation. Policymakers also track an even more granular metric, known as “supercore” inflation. It measures prices for core services once housing costs are excluded. For a second-straight month, it came in hot, rising 0.4 percent in September. Over the past three months, supercore prices have risen at an annual rate of nearly 4.6 percent. Those price gains will reinforce the central bank’s [view](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/business/fed-minutes-show-officials-saw-more-work-to-do-to-quell-inflation.html) that it will need to further tighten its grip on the economy to ease price pressures. So far, officials have argued that they can take their time before raising borrowing costs again, but September’s higher-than-expected inflation report will keep pressure on them to contine tightening. That was the message from the U.S. government bond market. The 2-year Treasury yield rose sharply by 0.1 percentage point to 4.88 percent in the wake of the report.

*   **Future moves:** The Fed will convene two more times before the end of the year, with the next meeting scheduled in late October just days before the midterm elections. Traders in federal funds futures markets still overwhelmingly expect the next rate increase at the Fed’s final gathering of the year in December. The need for further increases after that point will depend on how quickly inflation eases, as policymakers expect in 2027. In an [interview](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/fed-s-williams-currently-sees-no-need-for-rate-hike-in-2027) with Bloomberg on Tuesday, John C. Williams, who as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York is vice-chair of the policy-setting committee, said that while he still saw one more rate increase as appropriate this year, he did not expect further adjustments to be necessary after that.

Ben Casselman contributed reporting.

[![Image 2: Kevin Draper](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2018/07/18/multimedia/author-kevin-draper/author-kevin-draper-thumbLarge.png?quality=75&auto=avif)](https://www.nytimes.com/by/kevin-draper)

The Democratic candidate in the competitive Senate race in Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, is targeting his Republican opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, over the spike in energy prices. “Roger Marshall is to blame for the rising cost of fuel and inflation that’s costing Kansans hundreds more a month on everything from groceries and housing to healthcare,” Hamilton said in a statement, pointing to Marshall’s support for the Iran war and the president’s tariffs. The farming-heavy economy in Kansas has been hit hard by price increases.

Title: Rising Costs Push Necessities Out of Reach for Nearly Half of Americans - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/economy/high-prices-cost-of-living-pew-research.html

Published Time: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 14:31:58 GMT

Markdown Content:
Close to half of Americans are having trouble paying for basic needs, according to a [study by the Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/10/14/many-americans-are-struggling-to-afford-basic-necessities/), as the rising cost of living continues to exact its toll.

The financial burden is especially acute for lower-income adults. Nearly three-quarters said they struggled to pay for food, housing, medical care or daily transportation in the past year compared with 13 percent of upper-income adults. About half of those on the lower end of the income spectrum said they could not pay some of their bills each month, and 77 percent said they did not have enough money to cover expenses for three months in an emergency.

Black and Hispanic adults, women, young people and those without college degrees were more likely to say they faced financial challenges. Still, Americans across income levels, including 51 percent of wealthier adults, said they cut back in the past year on discretionary spending such as eating out and entertainment.

“We find consistently that these groups that are more likely to have lower family incomes are the ones who are struggling the most,” said Juliana Horowitz, senior associate director of research at the Pew Research Center.

The findings help illuminate the frustration over the economy that has become a defining issue heading into the midterm elections. Many Americans remain intensely anxious about their ability to afford daily life as stubborn inflation and higher gas prices brought on by the war in Iran continue to lift costs.

Views about economic inequality have changed as well, according to [another Pew study](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2026/10/14/americans-views-of-economic-inequality-its-causes-and-who-should-fix-it/). Roughly a quarter of people who said there was too much economic inequality also said the economic system needed to be completely rebuilt. That was up from 14 percent from 2019.

Democrats were almost twice as likely as Republicans to say there was too much economic inequality.

items.title: Social Security COLA for 2027 Will Be 3.6%
items.summary: The cost of living adjustment, or COLA, for next year will be the largest since 2023. Retirees will see the extra money in their benefit checks starting in January.
items.full_text:
Title: Social Security COLA for 2027 Will Be 3.6% - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/social-security-cola-retirees.html

Published Time: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 14:01:21 GMT

Markdown Content:
Retirees and other beneficiaries will receive the largest annual cost-of-living adjustment since 2023 in their Social Security checks next year, driven mainly by [persistently high inflation](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/pce-inflation-fed-interest-rates.html?searchResultPosition=2).

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6 percent annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, on Wednesday after the release of government inflation data for September. The COLA is determined using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The index values for July, August and September are averaged to produce the official adjustment figure.

For the average Social Security beneficiary, the COLA will translate to a $75 monthly increase, the government said. However, the actual amount for any retiree enrolled in Medicare will vary. The Part B premium, which covers outpatient care, is usually deducted from Social Security benefits, changing net COLAs. Separately, Social Security said the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax would rise to$192,300, up from $184,500 this year.

The Medicare board of trustees has projected that the monthly Part B premium will rise $6.60 in 2027 to $209.50. The final figure will be released this fall, but if the projection holds, most beneficiaries will receive net COLAs of at least 3 percent.

Other Medicare costs are rising, too. Monthly premiums for some [prescription drug plans](https://www.kff.org/medicare/many-medicare-part-d-stand-alone-drug-plan-enrollees-will-see-modest-premium-increases-for-2027-but-others-could-pay-much-more-if-they-dont-switch-plans/), which are known as Part D, will jump $50 or more next year — although plenty of lower-cost options are available for people who shop the market during the annual enrollment period that begins Thursday. In addition, [costs will rise](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/medicare-private-health-care-costs.html) and supplemental benefits will be reduced in private Medicare Advantage plans next year.

The CPI-W reflects price changes for goods and services that working people buy and use, and it is under-weighted for health care costs, which have an outsize impact on older Americans. The health spending burden for people enrolled in Medicare is more than twice as large as that of other households, accounting for [14 percent of total spending](https://8cmbykf0.r.us-east-1.awstrack.me/L0/https:%2F%2Fwww.kff.org%2Fmedicare%2Fkey-facts-about-health-care-affordability-for-people-with-medicare%2F/1/010001a1311a1da5-c40d42ca-9c53-4371-a8d1-c36eb1de8306-000000/YNSLf9mYyKWQ9lu1aZkteiU1d_M=473) in 2024, according to KFF, a health care research nonprofit.

The COLA announcement comes at a time when Americans are feeling less confident that they will have enough money to live comfortably in retirement. An annual survey released this year by the [Employee Benefit Research Institute](https://www.ebri.org/docs/default-source/rcs/2026-rcs/2026-rcs-release-report.pdf?sfvrsn=1229022f_1&utm_source=chatgpt.com) found that 61 percent of workers were confident they will have enough money to be comfortable in retirement, down from 72 percent in 2021; retiree confidence fell to 73 percent from 80 percent during the same period.

“For retirees who aren’t confident, inflation and the rising cost of living are overwhelmingly the top reason,” said Craig Copeland, director of wealth benefits research at E.B.R.I.

The automatic COLA is one of Social Security’s most valuable features, but some advocates have long argued that it isn’t adequate to help seniors cope with inflation — and that the CPI-W should be replaced by a yardstick that does a better job measuring the inflation that affects retirees.

A new AARP survey found that just 23 percent of adults over age 50 think a 3.5 percent COLA keeps up with rising prices. “For most people, the COLA just isn’t enough to keep up with what they see as rising costs in their life,” said Bill Sweeney, AARP’s senior vice president for government affairs. “When they go to the grocery store or fill up their tank with gas or get a notice that their rent is going up, it’s almost always higher than those numbers.”

Worries about the future of Social Security itself also are eroding confidence.

Social Security’s trustees [projected in June](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/09/business/social-security-benefits-cuts.html?searchResultPosition=2) that the retirement trust fund would be exhausted in 2032 — just six years from now. The combined retirement and disability funds are projected to run dry in 2034. Those are likely best-case projections, as key underlying factors have deteriorated over the past year, including lower long-range assumptions about the size of the U.S. population, which were affected by lower projections on the number of children women will have.

Trust fund exhaustion does not mean Social Security would stop paying benefits altogether, but it would set off an [across-the-board cut](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/business/social-security-income-retirement-benefits.html?searchResultPosition=1) of about 22 percent for retirement benefits in 2032, absent congressional action, according to the Social Security trustees. The top concern for retirees in this year’s E.B.R.I. survey was possible government changes.

“People are realizing that they’re going to have to make adjustments in their expectations of what the benefits are going to be in the future,” Mr. Copeland said.

The AARP survey found that 46 percent would cut back on dining out if benefits were reduced 5 percent — but a nearly equal share, 45 percent, said they would have to cut back on groceries and basic household items.

Retirement savings and investments can help plug the gap in meeting living costs, but those savings are available mainly to higher-income people. Among households ages 55 to 64 that have a 401(k) account, the median balance for the lowest fifth in 2022 was just $25,000 — and $220,000 in the third fifth, according to the [Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.](https://crr.bc.edu/401k-ira-holdings-in-2022-an-update-from-the-scf/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

At the same time, poverty rates for the lowest-income households are rising. The [Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2026/demo/p60-290.html) reported recently that the rate of poverty for Americans 65 and older rose to 15.4 percent in 2025 — the highest rate for all age groups, and up sharply from 12 percent in 2019.

The Social Security Administration will notify recipients about their new benefit amounts by mail and [online](https://www.ssa.gov/myaccount/) starting in early December, and the COLA will be added in January to the benefits of millions of Americans, a group that includes retirees and their spouses and survivors, as well as those who receive disability benefits and Supplemental Security Income.

Some older people also will receive a separate one-time payment of $90 this month from the government. [Characterized by the Trump administration](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/10/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-announces-medicare-improvement-fund-payments-for-seniors/) as a Part B “premium rebate,” the payment will be sent by direct deposit or check to 21 million people enrolled in Part B under traditional fee-for-service Medicare. The payments, before the midterm elections, were described by the White House as a “historic action to help senior citizens,” but [KFF noted](https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/the-trump-administrations-90-payment-to-medicare-beneficiaries-reminiscent-of-a-similar-proposal-six-years-ago-may-not-offset-rising-costs/) that the 2027 projected Part B premium increase alone would consume most of the $90 — and that less than half of all beneficiaries will get it, since Medicare Advantage enrollees are ineligible.

“An extra $90 in the bank won’t hurt,” said Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the program on Medicare policy at KFF. “But it’s not likely to stretch very far to cover higher costs for everyday essentials like putting food on the table, filling up the gas tank and paying the utility bill.”

A new alliance seeks legislation to force the biggest entertainment and streaming companies to devote half of their content budgets to independent producers in the U.S.

![Image 4](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/business/INDIE-TV-seinfeld-grid-1/INDIE-TV-seinfeld-grid-1-square640-v3.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif)

Shows like, clockwise from top left, “The Mary Tyler Moore Show,” “Roseanne,” “Seinfeld” and “Hill Street Blues” all came from independent producers.

CBS Photo Archives, ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content, via Getty Images, Photofest, Joey Delvalle/NBCUniversal, via Getty Images

Oct. 14, 2026, 9:00 a.m. ET

In the 1970s and ’80s, during a golden age of independent television production, series like “Hill Street Blues,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show,” “Seinfeld,” “Roseanne” and “St. Elsewhere” made their way to American living rooms. Those shows appeared on CBS, ABC or NBC, but thanks to government regulations, they were owned by companies and studios unconnected to the networks that aired them.

Since those regulations — the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules, or Fin-Syn — were repealed in the 1990s, many entertainment companies started airing and streaming programs from studios they owned, making it harder for independent producers to stay in business. Now, amid a painful, four-year downturn in the entertainment industry, there is a renewed push to bring back a form of Fin-Syn for the streaming age.

This week, a new organization called the American Entertainment Alliance will begin publicly pushing for legislation to force the biggest entertainment and streaming companies — including Netflix, Disney, Amazon Prime Video and Skydance — to allocate half of their original content budgets to shows and movies from independent producers in the United States.

The group’s supporters believe that if the biggest streamers buy a sizable share of programming from outside their own companies, it will reignite the television marketplace, increase the volume of TV shows made, expand opportunities for work and unleash a creative renaissance. If passed, the legislation could also provide bigger paydays for the top producers who create hit shows.

The organization is made up of some of the biggest players in Hollywood, including a rare coalition of rival talent agencies like the Creative Artists Agency, William Morris Endeavor and the United Talent Agency. The group also includes dozens of producers, including Jason Blum, Mark Burnett, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer.

“There are fewer people deciding what gets made and what we all see, what the consumer sees,” said Bryan Lourd, the chief executive of CAA. “This change that we’re putting forth would foster an environment where more things could get financed and therefore there’d be more storytellers, more jobs created. Distribution is not the issue of the future. Who finances content is the issue.”

Or as Mr. Grazer, a producer behind “Apollo 13,” “Arrested Development” and “Friday Night Lights,” put it: “We don’t want the media business to die.”

Getting any bipartisan legislation through Congress is, of course, no easy task. Many of these entertainment and streaming companies have large lobbying operations in Washington and are likely to fight any bill. The companies will argue that they already buy plenty of series and movies from outside studios.

In recent months, Hollywood has turned to Congress and President Trump to help stabilize the entertainment industry. In September, [a bill was](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/movies/film-tax-credit-congress-bill.html) introduced that would offer federal tax credits to encourage a return of production to the United States. The alliance’s efforts are different from that tax-break initiative, “but they are both necessary in order to fix what’s wrong,” Mr. Lourd said.

Since the Peak TV-era bubble burst, research indicates that the number of dramas, comedies and limited series has declined roughly 40 percent compared with four years ago.

Image

![Image 5: Ron Howard wearing a baseball cap that says Imagine on it.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/INDIE-TV-Ron-Howard-cjhg/INDIE-TV-Ron-Howard-cjhg-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Ron Howard, whose films include “A Beautiful Mind,” is a member of the new American Entertainment Alliance.Credit...Tom Jamieson for The New York Times

The alliance’s efforts began months ago, and were spearheaded by Chris Silbermann, a CAA managing director whose clients include Shonda Rhimes (“Grey’s Anatomy,” “Bridgerton”) and Vince Gilligan (“Breaking Bad”).

“The whole goal here is to get that ecosystem to thrive again,” Mr. Silbermann said.

Dan Limerick, the chief operating officer at WME, said, “To do nothing is not an option.”

Enter Fin-Syn. In the 1960s, regulators started looking skeptically at the television landscape, and were concerned with the concentration of power among the three big networks. (Fox began in 1986.)

The Fin-Syn rules came into effect in the early 1970s and largely prohibited the networks from acquiring ownership stakes from the independently produced series they aired in prime time. Soon, an entire ecosystem of independent producers and studios started to thrive, including MTM Enterprises (“The Mary Tyler Moore Show,” “St. Elsewhere”), Tandem Productions (“All in the Family,” “Good Times”), Lorimar (“Dallas,” “Knots Landing”), Carsey-Werner (“The Cosby Show,” “Roseanne”) and Castle Rock (“Seinfeld”).

The Federal Communications Commission [repealed the rules](https://www.nytimes.com/1993/04/12/business/the-media-business-television.html) in the 1990s because, in theory, the ascent of cable channels was providing more than enough competition for the networks.

Fast-forward to present day and the industry is confronting an entertainment landscape dominated by a handful of media and tech companies, and much of what they program they either own or refuse to let off their platforms for many years, members of the alliance said.

“Streamers collect the subscription fees and the advertising, and they own the shows,” said Mr. Burnett, the producer behind reality shows like “Survivor” and “The Apprentice.” “Isn’t it reasonable for some version of Fin-Syn to return where the creators of the shows have more ownership of those shows?”

In addition to forcing the companies to dedicate half their budgets to content from U.S. independent studios or producers, the alliance wants licensing and syndication rights for a TV show or a movie to revert to the production company or the outside studio after a few years. This would give a producer an opportunity to sell the movie or back seasons of a show elsewhere, and could provide a good payday.

The F.C.C. used to oversee the Fin-Syn rules, but given that the agency has little regulatory control over streaming platforms, the alliance is seeking legislation. Members have been in touch with sponsors of the federal tax credit bill, and are hoping to get a bill introduced next year.

Mr. Blum, who runs Blumhouse (“Get Out” and “The Purge”), a studio long seen as a symbol of success among independent producers, said that “we shouldn’t be this like singular thing — there should be a hundred Blumhouses.”

“I really believe that stifling or pushing independent companies out of business is ultimately bad for everyone,” he continued. “It’s bad for the consumer. It’s really bad for the platforms, too. It’s really hard to get ‘Get Out’ without an independent production company. It’s impossible to get ‘Obsession’ without an independent production company.”

Many producers pointed to the fact that other countries, including Britain, Germany and France, have similar rules.

Mr. Howard, who runs Imagine Entertainment (“A Beautiful Mind,” “Arrested Development”) with Mr. Grazer and Justin Wilkes, said the Fin-Syn rules had been critical for him to get his start in producing. He also said he had been “dying for the Fin-Syn rules to return” for more than two decades.

“Creatives are not at their best when they’re looking over their shoulder wondering if the bosses are going to like it,” Mr. Howard said. “They’re at their best when they’re incentivized, they have some agency and a reason to fight for ideas that they believe in. The marketplace then makes a determination, and that creative competition leads to real growth.”

[John Koblin](https://www.nytimes.com/by/john-koblin) covers the television industry for The Times.
